source.title: ShapleyLaw: A Game-Theoretic Approach to Multilingual Scaling Laws
source.authors: Xu-Yang Cao; Qian-Ying Liu; Chuan Xiao; Yusuke Oda; Jia-Ying Wang; Pontus Stenetorp; Daisuke Kawahara; Makoto Onizuka; Sadao Kurohashi; Shu-Yuan Zheng

page_placements.theme: Mixture composition, transfer and interference depend on scale

record.file_problem: The paper is present in full. Some extracted content in Appendix C.3, including Figure 10, is garbled.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates whether a multilingual scaling law predicts held-out pretraining loss, including at a larger model size, using a game-theoretic transfer measure rather than reproducing the original scaling-law method. It also tests the relationship between pretraining loss and downstream accuracy.
record.gate_note: The study reports language-mixture optimization results, Shapley-value transfer estimates, normalization comparisons, and architecture configurations. These do not directly test the listed versions about parameter-token compute-optimal allocation, architecture shape at fixed parameter count, or exponents and compute-optimal splits. The reported downstream mixture-optimization accuracies do not measure the relationship between downstream performance and scale or pretraining loss.
record.test_reason: The study fits a Chinchilla-form law, multiplied by a mixture term, on 50M–1460M multilingual models. It checks predictions on held-out larger runs (1460M and 3171M non-embedding parameters, D = 100B), which bears on V2. It also fits downstream accuracy against pretraining loss across mixtures, which bears on V6. The setting is new (language-mixture-aware multilingual pretraining) rather than a replication of the original method, so T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also claim that ShapleyLaw beats FamilyLaw and other baselines in loss prediction and mixture optimisation under real pretraining. They claim it extrapolates accurately to 3.2B models, and that cheap IRDS-approximated Shapley values preserve fitting quality.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes a game-theoretic multilingual scaling law using Shapley values to represent cross-lingual transfer and evaluates language-mixture prediction and optimization. It uses a Chinchilla scaling-law component but does not reproduce the original studies' scaling-law analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: The study compares Shapley-value normalization schemes: its softmax-like normalization has the lowest or tied-lowest prediction error for all seven evaluated languages (Table 11). It also reports language-specific variation in IRDS approximation effects (Appendix C.6).

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed N and D, per-language loss depends on the language mixture. A power law in SV-weighted aggregate transfer Θ predicts unseen random mixtures at 243M (PEtest 0.002–0.008). FamilyLaw fails here (R² ≤ 0, versus 0.931 for ShapleyLaw).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multilingual pretraining loss at fixed scale follows a power law in a transfer-weighted mixture variable.

fits_no_version.finding: Normalised Shapley transfer matrices at 50M and 243M are nearly identical (cosine 0.999; 0.995 off-diagonal).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-lingual transfer coefficients are stable across model scale.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The main text validates up to N = 1460M, with the larger N = 3171M test reported in the appendix. The tested scale range and extrapolation are limited relative to the claim's several-orders-of-magnitude scope. Prediction-error uncertainty intervals are not reported.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the tested versions. Results on mixture optimization, Shapley-value similarity, and normalization alternatives were not entered as rows because they do not measure the behavior specified by the tested claim versions.

untested.parts: Extrapolation over orders of magnitude: the largest held-out jump is ~2.2x in parameters (1460M→3171M). Data size is fixed at 100B, so extrapolation in tokens or compute is not tested.
Predictability of downstream performance directly from scale, and from loss at sizes other than 1.46B. The 243M random-mixture results are shown only in a figure.
No separate power-law fit of loss in N, D or compute is reported; N spans 50M–3.2B with D fixed.

missing.what: Held-out 1460M PEtest for English 0.004, French 0.013, German 0.012 and Korean 0.011 (curated mixtures). R² is 0.985–0.998.
Low-resource languages (Finnish, Croatian, Malay) held-out 1460M prediction. Malay PEtest = 0.047 is the largest error; Finnish and Croatian values are hard to read from the extraction.
English downstream fits over six tasks: Pearson −0.909 to −0.997, R² 0.843–0.996. Also Chinese/Japanese tasks and 50 random-mixture 243M models, shown only in a figure.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Extrapolation is small (~2x in N, D fixed), so the V2 support is narrow. The 1460M curated held-out points may not be pure extrapolation: the figure legends list N=1460M among the scales but only the 1460M points as held out. The downstream R² values are inconsistent across Tables 2, 7 and 8.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test power-law loss scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute with the other variables held non-bottlenecked over several orders of magnitude. Its multilingual loss model includes a Chinchilla-based component, but its experiments focus on language-mixture effects and prediction.

The study tests multilingual held-out prediction, including a held-out 3.171B-parameter scale, but does not establish prediction over several orders of magnitude or test the original scaling laws across broad parameter, token, and compute ranges.
It optimizes language mixture ratios, not the parameter-count and token-count split at a fixed compute budget.
Architecture details change with model scale, but the study does not compare architectures at a fixed parameter count.
The study concerns multilingual text pretraining and does not test other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer regimes.

It tests downstream accuracy against pretraining loss for selected multilingual NLU benchmarks and languages, but does not test a general relationship across downstream tasks or predictability directly from model scale.

It compares some Shapley-value normalization schemes, but does not test whether fitted scaling exponents or parameter-token compute-optimal splits depend on setup, nor whether scaling curves bend away from a single power law.
